The Prisoner and the Podcasters

“I want you to understand what it means to lose your freedom.”

He said that five times in a speech to a Bitcoin conference. He gave it over a collect call from a maximum security penitentiary.

Every few minutes an automated voice cut in over him:

"This call is from a federal prison."

He told them about the hole…

He once spent four months straight in there. He had air… stale and foul, but air. Food through a slot in the door. Other than that, it was just a lifeless hole.

And the hole wasn't the worst of it. It was the knowing that even once you're out of the hole, you're still not free… and you never will be again.

He was given two life sentences plus 40 years, with no chance for parole.

This is hell.

You can't even escape it in your dreams, when you sleep…

"In the dream I was free. I was in a park, and I felt this huge relief… and then the anxiety just woke me up. And there I was again, in the hole… Life without parole. Maximum security. There's no end in sight."

He knew what talking to that crowd might cost him. He told them so.

"I'm afraid that because of what I'm saying to you today, I'll be thrown in the hole, or worse."

He was right. That's exactly what they did.

His name is Ross Ulbricht.

On the night of September 10th, 2026, an arena in Dallas went silent. One year to the day since Charlie Kirk was assassinated.

One seat was left empty. An American flag was draped across it, and a white card sat on the chair:

"Saved for Charlie."

They played a five-minute video of him, and the whole arena stopped talking.

Then they started chanting his name.

"Charlie! Charlie! Charlie!"

Charlie was a big part of why Ross was free. He never took credit for it.

The morning after Charlie was killed, Ross told the world.

After the 2024 election, Trump asked Charlie what the number one thing he could do for him was. Charlie said: "Free Ross."

"At 31, my life was taken from me for standing up for what I believed in. And Charlie helped me get it back."

~ Ross Ulbricht, Sept 11, 2025

Less than an hour after the crowd chanted Charlie's name, Ross took the stage.

"When you are in prison, there is a certain sound that a steel door makes when it closes behind you and you are locked inside. I heard that sound every day for over 11 years."

Five years ago, he told a crowd of libertarians and Bitcoiners what it means to lose your freedom… over a prison phone.

Now he was telling an arena full of Republicans… as a free man.

He thanked the man who freed him:

"Thank you, Mr. President. You gave me my life back, sir."

He meant it. You can hear him choking back tears.

Trump had made a promise at the Libertarian National Convention in 2024… to a crowd that booed him from the moment he walked out. Some turned their backs on him. People held up signs:

"Free Ross"

He told them that if they voted for him, on Day 1, he would commute Ross's sentence to time served.

For one line, the room cheered… then they went back to jeering.

Trump kept the promise. More than that… he didn't just commute the sentence, he granted Ross a full pardon on his second day in office.

He didn't need the libertarians anymore. He'd already won. He did it anyway.

When he signed the pardon, he called Ross's mother, and said he'd done it "in honor of her and the Libertarian Movement." Then he posted that the people who convicted Ross were "some of the same lunatics" behind the weaponization of government against him.

He wasn't just letting a man out of prison. He was telling Ross and every libertarian who fought for him: we're in this together.

Ross understood:

"He felt compassion for me because he, too, was a target of a weaponized government."

Then he brought up his fellow libertarians.

"Now, sometimes I hear from the very people he made that campaign promise to… that after he freed me, he lost focus on the cause of liberty."

Ross is being generous with the word "sometimes." The truth is, many of the biggest libertarian influencers have their knives out for the one man who actually freed him… and for the coalition that stood behind him.

And look… some of their anger is earned. I'll get to that.

The night Ross walked free in January 2025, the Libertarian Party's 2024 presidential nominee, Chase Oliver, refused to thank Trump for it. Trump, he wrote, had "prioritized renaming the Gulf of Mexico over his Day 1 promise."

The pardon came one day late.

A year and a half later, on the morning of Ross's speech, the Libertarian Party's official account called Trump a "true Communist."

Even Dave Smith, who played a critical role in getting Ross freed. Two days after Massie lost his primary, he went on a panel show and declared war:

"Now, I'm just one guy, but I am fairly influential with some of the most influential people in this country… You've made an enemy out of the libertarians, and now enjoy."

~ Dave Smith, Brad Polumbo's panel, May 21, 2026

Four months later, on his podcast he played a clip of Ted Cruz saying Republicans need libertarians to show up in November. His answer:

"So, sorry Ted, we will not be coming out for you. You cannot count on libertarians in droves to save the Republicans in the midterms. I have a feeling you guys are going down."

~ Dave Smith, Part of the Problem, Sept 23, 2026

He told you himself: he's influential, and he knows it. That's a flex.

Dave has a giant audience, that's true… but he's mistaking it for power.

That audience couldn't save Massie, who lost by ten points. It couldn't free Ross without Trump… it couldn't even win Clint Russell the Libertarian VP nomination… and the only thing it can do now is help the Progressive coalition win.

Whether he means to or not, that's what he's doing.

So is Clint.

That same night, a few hours after Ross spoke, Trump joked from that same stage that if you don't vote, "you go to hell." Clint's reply:

"We're already in hell and I fully intend to take the GOP with me."

~ Clint Russell, X, Sept 11, 2026

Ross knows what hell is.

In 2021, Clint sat down with Ross's mother, Lyn, for an episode called "Free Ross!!!" He called it the most important episode he'd ever done.

Five years later, Ross stood in an arena and answered the libertarians himself.

Clint hasn't said a word about it on his show. Neither has Dave. I checked. I went through every episode either of them has put out since Ross's speech.

As far as they're concerned, it never happened.

And on September 25th, still angry about Massie, Clint posted this to the Republicans:

"…we're gonna make it very clear that you can't win without us. Fuck. All of. You."

~ Clint Russell, X, Sept 25, 2026

"All of you" includes Ross now, Clint.

Think about what that means. If Dave and Clint get their way, the coalition that freed Ross loses power in November… and it goes to the party that put him in that cell.

Back in June, I asked this question in "The Thomas Massie Problem":

"I cannot stop wondering what Ross thinks of these supporters right now. What does the man getting his life back think of his loudest defenders trying to destroy the man who gave it to him? … They know whose signature is on the pardon."

~ The Thomas Massie Problem, June 1, 2026

Now I have my answer.

Ross is standing right beside the man who signed it.

And to the people who say Trump lost focus on liberty, Ross answered them:

"That's not true. It's just easy to miss all of his wins for liberty among the torrent of headlines out there."

Then he listed them:

Hundreds of ordinary Americans pardoned, people you've never heard of.

"The government pushed banks to debank Americans for what they believed, or where they shopped… or for using Bitcoin. People lost their businesses not for breaking a law, but for being the wrong sort of citizen."

Gun dealers who lost their licenses over paperwork, back in business.

Veterans with severe trauma, finally allowed medicine the government had criminalized for half a century.

Social media companies no longer pressured by the federal government to silence Americans for what they say online.

Parents who spoke up at school board meetings no longer treated like terrorists.

This is practically a libertarian wish list, and almost nobody's talking about it… least of all, the libertarian podcasters.

He ended his speech like this:

"I stand here tonight a free man and you are free Americans. And that is thanks to him."

So here we are, libertarians. You have a choice to make this November.

I'm not going to sit here and lecture you about Trump. He's done some things I can't defend. I'm not going to tell you you're wrong about Iran. Or the spending.

You were courted in 2024. You showed up.

And then Trump went and did some very unlibertarian things. You got a war you didn't want. A spending bill that makes you sick…

And then your favorite congressman, the most principled libertarian in Congress, got taken out.

You felt like you were being told to see yourselves out.

I get it. I'd be angry too. You're even right about a lot of it.

But being right was never your problem.

"Power is what makes ideas matter. Without power, you don't have ideas… you have a hobby."

~ The Losertarian Problem, May 3, 2026

Ross is the proof. More than a decade of being right didn't open his cell. Power did.

I don't want you to lose anymore. I want you to win. Ross is what winning looks like. It's ugly… it's not perfect… far from it, but it's real. He's free.

Back in May, I gave you a test:

The libertarian test is the simplest possible question. Are you going to help Trump in the midterms or not?

Are you going to swallow your pride and vote Republican in your district? Or are you going to perform purity, vote third party, sit it out, and let the progressives take Congress back?

That is the test. The jokers will fail it. The serious libertarians will pass it.

Which one are you?

~ The Losertarian Problem, May 3, 2026

I'll be honest… I was worried Ross would fail. He's a libertarian, after all. They're loyal to principles, not people… and Trump is no libertarian.

He passed. Even with the loudest voices in his corner telling everyone Trump had betrayed them.

Now it's your turn.

One coalition put Ross in a cage he was never supposed to leave alive. The other set him free.

One saved Charlie a seat. You saw what the other did.

Ross is you. Charlie is you.

On November 3rd, stand beside Ross, with the coalition that freed him.

Vote Republican for your House seat. Especially if it hurts.

“I want you to understand what it means to lose your freedom.”

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: tomorrow! tomorrow!
preview: the real reason i've been singing all day...
html:
Tomorrow! Tomorrow! I’ll love ya… tomorrow… It’s only a day away.

Genuinely one of the greatest songs ever written, in my opinion. My sister drilled this one into my head from a young age… she was in a theater group, and they were doing a production of Annie.

It's one of those songs I like to pluck on the guitar whenever I pick it up. Brightens my day, immediately. This morning, I was humming it on a walk. Then I sang it in the shower.

And now here I am… singing it to you, in an email. You might be thinking it's because my next piece is coming out tomorrow. That's part of it.

But the bigger part is hope. The song is about hope… and there's a lot of doomer talk out there right now. Things look grim for Trump and Republicans in the midterms if you watch the media and the discourse around it.

The people who bet money on elections give Democrats a 90% chance of winning the House.

The polls look bad… and Mark Halperin is reporting that the GOP's private polling is even worse…

But you're not living behind the Iron Curtain in the 1960s, are you? You're not dead yet… right?

The sun is still going to come out tomorrow. Then it's going to come out the day after that. And for as long as that sun keeps coming out, there is hope.

And so, I'm not giving up.

Tomorrow, I publish the final part of my libertarian trilogy.

It's my case for why libertarians should show up for Republicans in November.

Part one: The Losertarian Problem

Part two: The Thomas Massie Problem

Part three: The Prisoner and the Podcasters.

Patrons are reading it right now. For everyone else, it unlocks tomorrow here: stopbeingprey.com/prisoner

Here are a few comments from patrons, so far:

"Take a bow, brother! Awesome new piece." ~ Sue

"From a recovering libertarian, this is not only a must read, but a must act piece." ~ Walker

"I voted Libertarian since before Ross was jailed. Didn't make a bit of difference… Then I voted for Donald. He kept his promise. Things changed." ~ Tim

The rest of my week will be spent trying to get this thing in front of libertarians. It is a persuasion piece. A weapon that I built for the midterms… but a weapon is no good if no one uses it.

So use it. Get it in front of people… especially libertarians. Force the question upon them, gracefully… "are you going to help… or sit this one out?"

I'm also trying something new. Something I've talked about in the past. Something I think your Founding Fathers would approve of. A flyer.

One page, the opening of the piece, and a QR code to scan for the rest. Print a few and hand them out. Look for it in your email tomorrow.

That's it. I'm going to get back to work. Lots to do to prepare.

In the meantime… don't get consumed by the doom and gloom being sold to you in the media right now.

Tomorrow, tomorrow… it's only a day away.

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: weapons
preview: i'm not talking about guns and knives
html:
Last night, six strangers prayed for a man who laughed at Charlie Kirk's murder.

He came into my comments swinging. He was nasty, he was mean... he was celebrating the murder of a young father. He wasn't a bot, he was a real guy... real friends, a real life... doesn't seem like that bad of a guy, really... minus the whole celebrating-a-murder thing.

But there he was... looking for a fight.

And some of my readers gave it to him. They matched his energy and became nasty and mean themselves.

I get it... I felt it too. I feel it all the time. I read dozens of comments like Daniel's every day... I can't post about Charlie without a series of people just like Daniel coming into the comments to pick a fight with my readers.

I'm not even saying that you shouldn't fight him. What I'm saying is this: don't fight on his terms. Fight on your own.

In the old days, when a man was challenged to a duel, he got to choose the weapons. It was a code of conduct. They called it the Code Duello.

Part of the idea was to discourage bullying. A skilled swordsman couldn't pick fights with weaker men and win easily, because they'd choose pistols.

Daniel is the skilled swordsman. His skill is making you angry, and he's very good at it. He knows exactly what to say to get you fired up... and you won't be able to do the same to him, no matter how hard you try to match his register. He's ready for it. He was expecting you.

So I chose a weapon he wasn't expecting. Well... two weapons, really.

Curiosity and Grace. Dual pistols.

Daniel got to fire the first shots... calling us clowns... laughing at us for mourning Charlie... posting a cartoon that makes a mockery of his murder.

I returned fire by giving him a warm welcome and asking him a genuine question.

And just like that... I took control of the entire conversation. I stayed on offense the whole time, while he spent the rest of the fight explaining himself... writing longer and longer answers with every shot of curiosity I fired. He still had his sword... he was trying to make me angry... insulting me, insulting Charlie, insulting my readers.

None of it landed. You can't wound a man who refuses to get angry.

By his third answer, he started wounding himself. I could tell he was starting to get angry. He wasn't laughing anymore.

So, I decided it was time to go for the kill. To settle this thing once and for all, so nobody, not even my haters, can deny who came out on top here.

I fired my second pistol. Grace.

I told him why I feel blessed. That I thank God every morning for my family, my friends... and even my enemies, who I cherish. That I see a lot of myself in him. That I'd pray for him.

I genuinely wish him well. You know why? I was an angry young man once. Mad at the world. Signalling my virtue by sneering at people I've never met, about issues I didn't really understand. I was spiteful. Resentful.

That's Daniel. I'm not Daniel anymore.

Maybe one day he won't be either.

And if he gets there, it won't be because someone out-argued him. It'll be because a bunch of strangers answered his hate with grace... we didn't feed into his resentment. We forgive him. We don't wish death upon him... we pray for his salvation. We don't let him bully us... we disarm him.

"Supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting."

~ Sun Tzu, the Art of War

This is what I want to teach you. This is the core of my Stop Being Prey doctrine: curiosity and Grace. I know you can see it. I know you have it in you. But sometimes, you follow your temptations. I still do too. It's an eternal struggle.

But that's the real fight... within you. Not against Daniel.

And here's the part Daniel never saw coming, when he came into my comments section, posting that cartoon of Charlie being murdered... that it would end with strangers praying for him. I dominated him with curiosity, and we devastated him with Grace, together.

This is how you win a fight like this. By choosing weapons that your enemy is not prepared for.

Charlie knew this... that's why they wanted him stopped. It works. It's persuasive. It can even cause your haters to look inside themselves and start asking tough questions.

I built Daniel a wall on my site. Anyone can leave him a message there, with a few dollars behind it.

Every dollar on that wall is taking Daniel's attack and turning it into fuel for the work he came to sneer at. Imagine what that does to Daniel when he sees that. He goes to the wall... sees a bunch of people praying for him, wishing him well... while funding the work of the guy he just publicly called trash.

What does that do to a man's conscience?

Let's find out. stopbeingprey.com/walls/bless-daniel

stay close,

~ Clay

P.S. Six strangers have left Daniel a message so far. Want to be the seventh? The wall closes Wednesday, when my libertarian piece goes out:
stopbeingprey.com/walls/bless-daniel

subject: daniel
preview: making my enemy work for me
html:
I'm a busy guy... I have a big piece coming out this week, and I have to develop a distribution and promotion strategy if I want it to actually get in front of the people who need to read it.

I don't really have time to be getting into fights right now.

But then Daniel showed up in my comments to celebrate Charlie's murder. To laugh at us and call us clowns for mourning him.

And so, I deployed one of my greatest weapons... curiosity.

The cat killer.

I didn't argue with him. I didn't get angry... I didn't try to prove him wrong, or call him evil.

I questioned him. I explored his thoughts with him. I was cordial throughout the whole thing... he even thanked me for that... then he called me trash, and a traitor in his next breath.

I walked him... one question at a time. Let him think he was leading. Just like when I walk my dog. The conversation went on for a while, and his replies got longer and longer with each question I asked.

In the end, he confessed his true feelings to us in explicit detail... he told us he feels blessed he wasn't born "stupid or hateful enough to become a Charlie Kirk supporter."

Below is my final reply to him.

Daniel... you came back! Thank you! I honestly was expecting you to leave me hanging on that question... I'm delighted, genuinely.

You told us you feel blessed every morning that you weren't born "stupid or hateful enough to become a Charlie Kirk supporter."

I appreciate you sharing that. It gives us great insight into who Daniel is.

I'd like to tell you why I feel blessed.

When I wake up in the morning, the first thing I do is thank God for all of the blessings in my life. My family, my friends, my career, my health, my dog... and even my enemies, who I cherish.

I cherish my enemies because they make me sharper. Every one of them teaches me something, and teaches my readers something too.

You taught us something too, Daniel. You showed us what it looks like when a normal, well-liked guy agrees with the man who killed Charlie. You posted all of this under your real profile, with real pictures of you and your friends. I saw the pictures of you guys camping... looks like fun. Reminds me of going camping with my friends.

I bet you and I could have fun together, Daniel. I bet we could get along...

I see a lot of myself in you. When I was younger, and felt cornered in an argument... I'd write longer and longer explanations, trying to convince myself as much as anyone else. Does that sound familiar, Daniel?

Somewhere along the way, someone taught you that Charlie was a man whose death was worth celebrating. I don't think you came up with that on your own. If you actually read the piece you're commenting on, you'd find yourself in it. I wrote it before I ever met you.

And so, what's my point?

Not much. I just want you to know that I see you, that I cherish you, and I will pray for you.

God bless you.

~ Clay

p.s. One more thing. You work for me now, Daniel. You're helping fund my work... isn't that awesome? People are going to send me money, and they're going to attach a message for you with every dollar. You did that for me. Thank you.

The messages will be publicly available if you want to watch them come in: stopbeingprey.com/walls/bless-daniel

That's my last word to Daniel. The rest is yours

Five dollars puts your message on the wall, where he'll see it. I'd suggest a blessing... that's what Charlie would've done.

A reader already left Daniel this: "Daniel, may you find the grace which opens up your heart to what is truly compassionate."

Yours can be next.

stopbeingprey.com/walls/bless-daniel

stay close,
~ Clay

subject: what killed the cat?
preview: it wasn't his curiosity
html:
Curiosity killed the cat. I must've heard that a thousand times growing up.

Every kid hears those words the moment they ask one question too many.

It's a way of shutting down conversation. It's not the cat being killed, it's your curiosity. Without it, you're just waiting to be told what to think.

So, who would tell you to stop being curious?

When you were a kid, it was the grown-ups. Maybe your parents, your teacher… some other authority figure. You'd ask why, and then why again, until you heard it... "because I said so!"

Now that you're grown up... it's the news anchors and the fact-checkers. "Conspiracy theorist." "Election denier." "97% of scientists agree."

It’s all the same trick. Stop asking and obey! You don't want to end up like that damn cat, do you?

There are a lot of people who'd prefer you stopped asking questions. Sometimes, you're that person. So am I.

When I'm in a heated argument about something I care about, I'm not curious about the other guy at all. I'm just waiting for my turn to talk.

I want revenge. I want to make them feel hurt, or embarrassed. I become angry and vindictive.

Sound familiar? Have you ever been that guy?

It doesn't have to go that way. You don't have to be defensive and reactive.

Try being genuinely curious about the other person's perspective.

Not the "just asking questions" kind, where the question is an accusation. Real curiosity, where you actually want to hear the answer and learn. Maybe there's something you missed, maybe this person has considered the issue from an angle you haven't.

What you will discover, as I have, is that most people haven’t really thought these issues through with any depth.

The people who preach the virtues of a $20 minimum wage have never thought about the question “Why not $50? Or $100?”

But, if you meet them with anger and resentment, instead of curiosity… “The minimum wage destroys jobs, only an idiot would believe in it!”

That's not a hunter. That's a cornered animal lashing out.

The moment you get angry, you stop hunting and become prey.

Curiosity didn't kill the cat. It's what separates the hunter from the hunted.

stay close and curious,

~ Clay

subject: i called them losers on purpose
preview: and it works every time I want it to
html:
I went out to get some lunch today. Three quarter pounder patties from McDonald’s.

No burger. Just the meat. I’m trying to minimize carbs right now, it’s a whole thing.

I had a podcast playing in my car. Michael Malice was interviewing Jesse Lee Peterson.

I’ll just admit upfront, that I’m a fan of both of these guys. They both make me laugh while they feed me surprisingly deep insights.

The episode started off with a bang.

Michael asked:

"Jesse, there's something you talk about all the time, and I'm sure at some point you feel like a broken record, but I wanna ask you about it again because this is the kinda thing where if people just listen to you, their lives will instantly become better from this show.

And that question is this: Why is anger so bad, and why is it so important for people to let go of anger?"

And Jesse responded:

"Anger is bad because anger is evil."

He made his case. He spoke about forgiveness, mothers, and the struggle to admit you're angry in the first place. He said that it doesn't matter how nice a man seems, or what church he attends… if he's angry, he's evil.

There’s a lot of angry people out there… and let’s be honest. Are you one of them? Sometimes, maybe? I know I am.

That’s evil, according to Jesse. And he has a point.

What has your anger done for you? When someone posts something online that makes you upset, and you write that comment from a place of rage… what good has that ever done you?

Nothing, and you keep doing it anyway.

Why? Was it your own choice? Did you wake up in the morning and decide “I think I’m going to be angry today!”… or did you get provoked?

I see it every day. Angry people in my comments, fighting with each other all day long.

And do you know what everyone who runs a large political social media account realizes eventually? Anger is what sells. That’s how you make money. Get attention. Engagement.

For example… Why do you think I spent so much time calling Libertarians losers? I called my piece “The Losertarian Problem”. It wasn’t just a clever title… it was something to provoke a reaction. To make libertarians angry.

It worked. It works whenever I want it to. I can go onto my page and post it again today, and I’ll have angry libertarians filling my comment section looking to pick a fight with me… by the thousands.

And I'm just one guy with a moderately successful Facebook page. I'm a small fish in this vast ocean… and the big ones all have staff and budgets.

There are people being paid big money right now, as I write this, to figure out what makes you angry, so they can point you where they want you.

And so, I don’t think evil is quite the right word here. I think I have a better one.

Prey.

When you are angry, you are prey. When the libertarians are angry at me calling them losers, they become my prey. They promote my article for me, to other libertarians in their feed. The exact people I’m trying to reach.

That’s the game.

So, the next time you feel anger… ask yourself… Did I choose this, or did somebody choose it for me? Who’s getting something out of this?

After listening to Jesse, I went looking for what the Bible actually says about anger. This passage from Proverbs 25:28 stuck out to me:

"He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls."

A city with no walls isn't wicked. It's just open.

subject: he wanted that smell in his fur
preview: and nothing was going to stop him
html:
Sometimes when I’m walking my dog, he’ll get on a scent. Something's out there, and nothing is going to stop him from finding it.

He pulls on my leash, I let his determination lead us. And what do we find? A smelly pile of decomposing flesh that he decided he needs to roll around in.

Before I even realize what’s going on, he’s covered in it.

He gets up, he looks at me like he just won something. Like he just did both of us a favor somehow.

He has no idea he just bought himself a bath, where he will shake helplessly, and look into my eyes with despair as I purge the stink from his coat. As if I’m the one being indecent here.

We’ve been through this before. Countless times.

He doesn’t learn. He never will.

He's a dog, he can't see past the scent… he runs on instincts.

You're not a dog.

What's your excuse? When some stranger's comment gets you all fired up on the internet… why are you so compelled to respond?

One of my readers, Kim, put it better than I can:

"Like I tell my dog, LEAVE IT."

She's right.

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: a frightened animal
preview: what you're really arguing with
html:
Alan, whose question I answered yesterday, wrote back. His first line was "I was afraid that was going to be your answer."

That's not exactly what I was hoping for, but it is the truth… and here, we deal with the truth, even if it's not what we want.

He told me about a friend of his. Not somebody online. A woman he's known for years. He describes her as very liberal.

He put a question to her. Not an accusation, just a possibility.

Could the people funding scientific studies be getting the conclusions they paid for? Is it possible that politics and money can corrupt science?

Her response:

"No, I could never accept something like that happening."

Alan is perceptive. He noticed that she didn't tell him it was false. She told him she couldn't accept it.

These are not the same thing.

In his words: she didn't just trust them, she had to.

Her brain didn't check whether it was true. It checked what it would cost if it were, and the price came back too high.

This is why the tape doesn't work. If you show someone the full context of the very fine people hoax, they'll still reject the evidence right in front of their eyes. They'll rationalize it… explain it away.

You’re asking whether it's true. They're asking a different question. "What is this going to cost me?"

No amount of evidence is going to do it. That's not how persuasion works.

The late great Scott Adams wrote a whole book about this. He called it Win Bigly: Persuasion in a World Where Facts Don't Matter.

Now… before you get too cocky… I want you to understand something. You do this too. We all have this tendency. It's innate.

When you really care about something, you feel the answer before you think it, don’t you? That flash of irritation when somebody questions it... that's the thing I need you to think about. Those are the moments when you start to make mistakes and fall for traps.

That's the animal instincts in you, reacting to a perceived danger. That's not the thinking part of your brain at work.

You can't control how other people react to danger. What you can do is notice it, in them and in yourself.

When you see that flash, you're not talking to the thinking part anymore, you're dealing with a frightened animal.

Alan ended his email telling me he gets depressed thinking about all this. I understand that. If evidence doesn't move anybody, what was the point of any of it?

Somewhere underneath that frightened animal is your friend. That's the point. That's who we're fighting for.

subject: arguing with the weatherman
preview: why your sister can't see it
html:
A reader named Alan wrote to me last night, in response to my email "enemy of the people", about the duplicity of the so-called "free press."

"What I can't quite put my finger on is why so many people insist on believing what they say, without question... But what about the built-in ability that most people seem to have to discern truth from falsehood? Why isn't that working? Surely liberal gullibility isn't the whole answer? What am I missing?"

It's a great question, because the easy answers fall apart the moment you think about the people you actually know.

I hear it all the time: "what a bunch of idiots"... but that doesn't explain anything... that's just an easy answer. It gives you a sense of catharsis to say it, but it explains nothing.

A smart man isn't harder to fool. Any good magician could tell you this.

A magician doesn't fool your eyes. He borrows your assumptions and plays with them... he tells you where to look, and you look. That's the whole job. Deception. Sleight of hand.

You're not wrong about what you saw... you're wrong about what you didn't.

Your mind goes looking for the part it missed... and if the magician is good, you won't find it. You'll know you were had, and you won't know how. That's the fun of a good magic show!

You are the mark, and you know it.

Now imagine if you didn't know it. There's no stage, you didn't buy a ticket… you just kicked your feet up at the end of a hard day's work and turned on the TV to get informed about what's happening in the world.

The president is on your screen. He says there were very fine people on both sides.

He said it. It's on tape… you can go watch it yourself. The Corporate Press played this clip relentlessly, for months… years even. They ran headlines, wrote articles, shared viral tweets… all based on this premise.

Do you remember?

It spread, like a virus. Biden launched his whole 2020 campaign on it. April 2019, Charlottesville front and center, those words quoted back at the country… "some very fine people on both sides".

And not one of them played what Trump said next.

"I'm not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists, because they should be condemned totally."

That was at the same press conference, in the same exchange… they cut it.

That's the trick. Do you see it?

Most people didn't… many still don't. Go talk to your liberal friends today, and there's a good chance they still believe the fine people hoax.

Michael Malice, one of my favorite authors, has a great line about this.

"the corporate press is factual but not truthful"

You can show them the tape. I have. It changes nothing... and that's the real question Alan was getting at.

"why so many people insist on believing what they say, without question"

Think about the weatherman. Imagine telling your neighbor the weatherman is lying to them... that there's a grand conspiracy to give people bad weather information, and the guy they trust on their TV every night is in on it.

They'd look at you like you're crazy... and they'd be right. The forecast is true. So is the traffic, so are the sports scores and the lottery numbers. Most of what they're watching on the news is completely true.

And that's what pays for the part that isn't.

The news earned that trust. Nobody goes back and verifies any of it, and why would they? It isn't their job. They have lives.

And then you show them the clip, and it doesn't land as proof. It lands as you looking strange about politics. Like you're arguing with the weatherman.

They're not idiots. They're the audience... and nobody told them there was a show.

What can you do about it?

Not much, honestly. And be honest with yourself... have you ever behaved like that? I know I have. When a story confirms my bias and comes from an authoritative source… I want to choose the path of least resistance and just accept it.

But we can't do that. Not if we want to be better.

"Don't trust, verify"

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: a graceful predator
preview: she stopped the fight in its tracks
html:
When you start viewing politics through a predator/prey lens, rather than a liberal/conservative or left/right one, you start to see things a bit more clearly. You start to feel the animalistic nature of everything. It isn't about the arguments, or the truth. It's about... something else.

It's about who controls the frame.

It's about who's hunting, and who doesn't realize they're being hunted.

Who is laying the traps, and who is getting trapped.

A reader sent me a story this week that shows it better than I could explain it.

Her name is Blanche. She lives in Arizona. Last year she flew to Connecticut to stay with her sister, who had just lost her husband.

Her sister prides herself on being very liberal. She's also a devout Catholic.

At dinner one night, Blanche mentioned she has a concealed carry license. Her sister was appalled.

"My Franciscan values tell me I would rather be murdered than kill someone else."

Blanche shrugged her shoulders and let it go. A perfect response, in my opinion.

Blanche continued:

"The following evening we were getting ready to turn in, and a conversation came up (I don't remember what exactly we were talking about), and I made the statement that the biggest lie perpetrated on modern society was that a fetus is the moral equivalent of a hangnail.

She went off like rockets. Yelling about a woman's right to choose, how Trump ruined everything, etc, etc. It was so sudden, I was startled.

I put my hands up and told her - NO, we are not doing this. I love you too much. You are too important to me - more important than fighting over this. I had to stop her several times, as she kept trying to talk.

When she finally stopped, she said 'I would really like to be able to talk to you about these things'. I said 'No you don't. You think that my opinion has no value because I don't agree with you.' She paused for a long while, and said 'It's true. You're right'."

Do you see what she did? That's frame control... firm, but graceful.

Most people have two options when that happens. Fight back, or shut up and take it. Both of those are reactionary prey behavior. You aren't setting the frame, you are under theirs.

Blanche did neither. She stopped the fight, in its tracks... and she claimed the authority to do so by describing it accurately.

"You think that my opinion has no value because I don't agree with you."

And her sister had nowhere to go. She had to deny it or admit it. She admitted it... which is to be commended as well... but it would not have been possible without Blanche's frame control.

If her sister controlled the frame instead, this would have ended very differently. It could have destroyed the relationship... I've seen it happen. Many of you have written to me about exactly this scenario.

Blanche didn't need to win the argument, because she was in control of whether or not there even needed to be one. She gets to keep her sister, and she never gave up an inch of what she believes.

So tonight, let's all tip our hat to Blanche... a graceful predator, showing us all how it's done.

stay close,

~ Clay

p.s. Blanche ended her email with this: "Although I may not comment a lot, I am learning a great deal." That's most of you. Quiet, reading, learning. I may not hear from you often, but I know you're out there. I'm rooting for you.

subject: nice guys need not apply
preview: I thought christianity was weak
html:
I've spent the morning reading your replies to yesterday's email. I didn't expect such a huge response. These weren't just short replies, you guys wrote entire stories to me. I haven't read them all yet, I'm working on it, but I promise you I will.

I can see that many of you are going through the same type of struggle as me.

I heard from a wife whose husband hasn't spoken to his own brother in over two years, over politics. A mother whose daughter stopped talking to her when Trump was elected.

But even more of you told me you've gone quiet. A wife who's kept her mouth shut in her own marriage since 2020, and says it's made her lonely. One of you said, "I feel like a coward."

And I realize some of you heard me say "keep your mouth shut." I can see how you got there from what I wrote. But to be clear, that's not what I meant.

Why do so many of us believe keeping quiet is the good thing to do? I think it's because we've confused being good with being nice.

Every man knows what it means when a woman he's interested in calls him a "nice guy." It means you were friend zoned. You're not mating material. It's a way of rejecting you without being mean about it.

When women call me nice… I take it harder than if they were genuinely trying to insult me. An insult at least means I made her feel something.

"Nice" means if something goes wrong, I'm not the guy she'd want next to her. I'm closer to a pet than a man. Something nice to keep around, but not something you can depend on.

Nobody wants to be the nice guy. So why do so many Christians try so hard to be one?

A lot of us were raised to believe keeping quiet is the Christian thing to do. Turn the other cheek. Keep the peace. Be nice.

For most of my life, this is how I viewed Christianity. The nice guy of religions. Completely submissive to those who exercise real power.

A hippie Jesus who never raised his voice, and would hug it out with anyone, about anything. As if he would show up to a Pride parade saying "love is love."

A socialist Jesus… he fed the hungry, so the government should too.

A refugee Jesus… who'd be against borders. "No human is illegal!"

A Jesus who never judges… he hung out with sinners, so nobody's really a sinner.

Harmless. Agreeable. A nice guy.

In Toronto, not far from where I was born, the Catholic school board voted to fly the Pride flag at every one of its schools, every June.

If this is what represents Christianity, then you might as well make Barack Obama the Pope. This version of Christianity was prey. Progressivism caught it, hollowed it out, and now wears its skin.

Now look at Islam. Does it have this problem?

A city in Michigan called Hamtramck became the first city in America with an all-Muslim city council. In June 2023, they voted to ban Pride flags from city property. Unanimously. Not a single person on the council was concerned about looking nice.

It went to court… and just last month, a federal appeals court said the ban stands.

So the Catholics raise the flag, and the Muslims take it down.

So should we all just convert to Islam then and be done with it? Join the winning team? No, of course not. But we do have a real problem with Christians feeling compelled to behave like prey, don't you think?

"Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword. For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother… And a man's foes shall be they of his own household." (Matthew 10:34-36)

Jesus never promised you peace at the dinner table. He warned you the truth would cost you, even with your own family and your own church. He told you to follow Him anyway.

For most of my life, I rejected Christianity because I thought it was weak. What else was I supposed to think? Look at the version that had been presented to me. No wonder young men walked away. They don't want to be someone else's pet... they want to follow the guy with a sword.

No one, and I mean no one in my extended friend group, took it seriously. Christianity wasn't something we thought about or talked about at all. Religion, to us, looked like silly nonsense for stupid people. I’m sorry to put it so bluntly, but this is how a lot of young people see it.

But that's not how I see it anymore. Thanks in large part to Charlie Kirk, and the example he set… I can see the sword. A faith that makes you choose a side, even when it costs you everything. I can see that good and evil are real… and that the war itself is being waged inside of our own hearts. It is a spiritual battle that we are in.

That doesn't mean picking fights with family at Thanksgiving. I meant what I said yesterday. But when the truth is on the line, you don't hide it to keep the peace.

You pursue the truth relentlessly… and the truth isn't nice. Nice guys need not apply.

stay close,
~ Clay

subject: I made the case for child labor
preview: my friends were not happy with me
html:
About a decade ago, shortly after I bought my first house, I had three friends come up to spend the night. It was supposed to be a night of fun and reminiscing about the great times we'd had.

I don't remember how it happened… but at some point things turned political and I found myself making the case for child labor.

I was still deep in my losertarian phase.

I unironically think it's good for kids to work, and believe child labor laws are far more destructive than they are helpful. I still believe this, by the way.

You can imagine how normal people receive this. Perhaps even you, dear reader, are recoiling in horror right now as I say it. That's okay.

For two of my three friends, this was the reaction. One of them, Brad, was a new father, so he was probably imagining his daughter in the coal mines or something, with me cracking the whip.

What I had in mind was more like this. If you gave me a choice as a kid… I had to either go to school for 8 hours a day, make no money, and be forced to do school work all day… OR get a real job, do real work, learn real marketable skills and make real money? You would've seen a Clay shaped hole in the wall of that school, like a Bugs Bunny cartoon… I would've left instantly.

But they didn't hear that. They heard something along the lines of "Clay wants to put kids back in the coal mines."

Andrew was the one who was really appalled, and he came after me hard. They tag-teamed me.

We were drinking… we argued. The volume escalated… I didn't back down or concede anything. I doubled down. So did they.

Needless to say, it was a miserable night.

The next day, we all woke up hungover… and they left. It was awkward. We were all friendly and cordial, but the damage was done. It honestly hasn't been the same since with two of them, and I blame myself for that. Not them.

In their defense, what I'm saying sounds crazy to most people, and it requires a careful approach if you want a real conversation about it.

I wasn't doing that. I was talking to them the way I talked to people online.

I wanted to 'own' them. I wanted to show I knew more, that I had done the reading and they hadn't. That I had thought this through, while they were just having a reaction.

I was arrogant… a know-it-all. I was angry. They could feel the negative energy coming off of me, and they returned it in kind.

The third friend, Brandon, just kind of observed and didn't participate.

He has since told me he thought I was the one being reasonable… the other two guys just weren't listening. In his mind, I was understandably getting frustrated.

Honestly, the fact that Brandon saw what I was really trying to say is something of a miracle…

Brandon is an odd character, like me. Immune to social pressures when it comes to political narratives… he's willing to say the things that get you ostracized from polite society if he feels they are right.

There's no one else in my life I can talk to like him. Not my parents, not my sister, not any of my other friends.

Most people are not Brandon.

I used to argue with anyone, any time, anywhere. I'd see people I love posting progressive nonsense on my Facebook feed and feel compelled to say something. To correct them in front of all their friends and family.

But there were no more Brandons who I was winning over. I was just doing damage to my relationships with nothing to show for it.

And so I stopped. Cold turkey. Like a drug addict kicking his habit to the curb.

I don't argue with friends and family about politics anymore, unless they come to me first…

Picking political fights with people you love almost never changes their mind. It just damages a relationship you valued.

Don't avoid it when it comes to you, but you don't need to go hunting for it at the dinner table or your feed.

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: there is no plan
preview: a reader of mine was there
html:
Yesterday was the 25th anniversary of 9/11.

I wanted to write to you about it.

I sat down at my computer and I really tried to come up with something, but all I could think about was an email I received back in June from a reader. It was a reply to my piece "It's Just a Shot Away", which you can read here.

He was a New York City firefighter. He was there that morning. What most of us saw on a TV screen, he saw with his own eyes. He breathed that polluted air with his own lungs.

I emailed him late last night to ask him if I could share his story with you, and he said yes.

These are his words exactly. I only broke them into paragraphs to make it easier to read.

For me, it was 9/11. At the time, I was a NYC Firefighter. I was working at headquarters right over the bridge from where the first plane hit.

A bunch of guys were mustering in the lobby. They had planned to walk over the bridge and do what they could. There was a lot of yelling, questions, in particular, "what are we going to do about gear and equipment?!" The answer was, "don't worry about it, we'll figure it out when we get there!"

The plan ultimately was, there is no plan.

At that moment, I decided to get in my truck and drive to the Bronx, where I was regularly stationed, to get my gear and return to the WTC.

While I was stuck in traffic trying to get to the Bronx, the south tower collapsed in full view of the cars traveling in the opposite direction. The look of pain, horror and sadness on the faces of those drivers while pointing at the collapsing building are seared in my mind. I looked in my side view mirror to see the remnants of the south tower disappear.

Ultimately, all the men who mustered in the lobby perished.

Long story short, I had survivors guilt, bad. PTSD, bad. But the moment that building collapsed was my moment. I knew nothing would ever be the same.

After weeks of digging up body parts, my crew found a fire lieutenant that was well known. I felt a bit of weight off my shoulders. We gave closure to his family that many others still don't have to this day.

But ever since, I've felt like that shot away.

One day, I was interviewed some months later by a small local paper while I was working. I remember telling the reporter when she asked me how I felt currently. I remember saying that all our problems felt smaller after that day. That I held my family tighter.

That was the kiss away, for me.

After what I had put my family through for months, after we found Ray Murphy, things started to get better just a little bit, day by day. I still don't remember the things I did to my family, how I yelled at them for nothing all the time. My wife told me she was scared, didn't know what to do. Zero recollection. But she stood by me.

Just a kiss away.

Thanks for that, man. I appreciate you.

Darren DeBonet

I wrote that essay in June.

It was about the Rolling Stones song "Gimme Shelter", and how close the worst thing and the best thing are to each other. Just a shot away from horror, just a kiss away from connection.

Darren read it and told me where both are in his life. The tower coming down was the shot. His wife standing next to him through the months he can't even remember was the kiss.

Pray for Darren today, and everyone else who faced down the hell he faced that day, 25 years ago.

stay close,

~ Clay

Do you ever think about your own death? I do… probably too often. I was thinking about it tonight, as I went for a walk through a grassy field in the pitch black of the night…

What are people going to say about me? What even was the point of my life? How long until I am completely forgotten, and the last person thinks of me for the last time?

I'm writing this email to you at about 10pm on September 9th, 2026. Just two hours before the anniversary of Charlie Kirk's murder.

I just stumbled upon a video in my feed of a young Charlie at a baseball game. He looks to be a teenager. And what does he say? "Hello. If you're watching this, I'm probably dead."

He was joking... he had a coy little smirk on his face as he said it… but now it's painfully real.

And tomorrow, it’s been one year.

One full year, and millions of people are still thinking about him and will be praying for his family tomorrow. Remembering his life. Sharing clips.

Even his haters keep his memory alive.

subject: paint grenades
preview: and they actually worked
html:
I LOVED school. The world seemed to be contained there.

That's what one of you wrote to me this morning.

Yesterday I told you school was a prison. I expected most of you would say the same. Some of you did. But my inbox also filled up with people telling me how much they loved it.

I get it. I respect it. I wish that was my experience, and I'm happy for you that it was yours.

This is new to me. I'm used to interacting with libertarians, and generally… they hate school. One of my favorite libertarian podcasts was literally called the "School Sucks Podcast."

My contempt for school is the most libertarian streak that remains within me.

For me, school was something much closer to torture. It was painful to be there. I dreaded it. I would lose sleep over it, I would pretend to be sick so I could stay home as much as possible.

My parents resisted this at first... I wasn't a great actor. But I was determined, and I wore down their will.

I was getting out of that prison, one way or another. I had an important meeting with Bob Barker and his Beauties to get to.

There are some fleeting moments I look fondly on.

My love for computer programming started in high school because of a teacher named Mr. Gay. I had him for one semester, and one class twice per week.

The other kids in that class treated it like it was just another thing to get through. Put your head down and learn it so you pass the test, get the credit and never think about Visual Basic again.

For me, it was the coolest thing I've ever done. The fact that I was actually learning how to write real computer software blew my mind.

I always loved computers, but I was more of a user… never a programmer. This was the first time I started to see computers as a tool. Something I could build with. Maybe even my future career!

Mr. Gay was a total nerd, and I mean that in the best possible sense of the term. He loved computers as much as I did, but unlike me, he knew how to build things with them.

And that's all he did. All day long, you'd either see him in a class teaching kids about computers, or in his off time he'd be doing all kinds of technical computer stuff in his little office.

He had a passion for it, and it fueled my own. I took his class more seriously than I ever took any class in my life.

At the end of the year, we had to build a final project… and we were free to build whatever we could think of.

I decided I was going to build a paintball game. It was an ambitious project well beyond the type of stuff we learned in the class.

I was the type of kid who never did homework. I didn't permit my teachers to have any claim to my time outside of school. But not this time… now my homework became my life. I did almost nothing else for a month.

I made the best damn game I could, and it blew Mr. Gay and his assistant away. It was a two-player game, so I invited another classmate up to play it for my demonstration. We shot each other with paintballs right there in front of the class. You could throw paint grenades, and they actually worked. I remember the other kid saying, "this is awesome."

They both gave me 110% on the project. Above perfect, they said. It was my crowning achievement in high school. I went home proud of myself in a way I'd never been before. I built a website on geocities for the game, and showed it off to friends and family whenever I got the chance. (who remembers geocities?!)

Mr. Gay took me aside at the end of the year and really encouraged me. “You’re good at this, you should think about going to school for it.”

But it was only Grade 11. I still had another year of public school to grind through.

A year of prison… forced to sit in classrooms with 30 other kids, while some government employee rattled off about something I didn’t care about for weeks upon weeks.

I never had Mr. Gay as a teacher again. I never had the option. I took computer science again a year later, but had a different teacher. One who didn't really give a shit.

He didn't encourage me and had no passion… it was just his job. He was going through the motions for a paycheck.

What really stings is I can remember passing Mr. Gay in the hall and saying hello, and he looked at me like he didn’t remember me at all.

I don’t blame him, he had hundreds of students over the course of the year… but it stung all the same.

And so, my passion for programming died for a while. A long while... and my contempt for the school system grew more profound than it ever was before.

It wasn't that I didn't want to learn.

I desperately wanted to learn.

I just wanted to learn something that mattered to me.

And I wanted somebody who gave a shit whether I did.

I can understand why you loved school. Can you understand why I hated it?

stay close,

~ Clay

p.s. A lot of you wrote to me about the alternatives. Charter schools, homeschooling, Sudbury Schools, unschooling. I'm more radical on this question than most. I’ll write more about that soon.

subject: three more episodes
preview: that's how we measured the school day
html:
I remember sitting there in class… it was maybe grade 3 or 4. The details are fuzzy, but I know I was there with my friend Brian. Neither of us were where we wanted to be.

Stuck in our crappy little desks on our stiff wooden chairs with 30 other kids in the room, trying to pretend like we were working so we wouldn't get in trouble. But we weren’t working. We were looking at the clock, dreaming about getting out of that place.

I remember how we would count time. We would think in terms of Simpsons episodes. “Only 3 more episodes until recess”… “Just one more episode and a few commercials until we get to go home.”

This might sound like a cute little story to you about my childhood, but for me it’s a bit infuriating to reflect on. I hated school. I mean HATED it. I still do.

I’m resentful about it. Not about any of the violence or bullying or any of those experiences, but of the boredom. The sheer boredom I was forced to face for 12+ years of my life. The most important years of my young life, snuffed out by putting me in a room I didn’t want to be in, around people I didn’t want to be around.

I don’t know what it’s like to be a kid in public school these days, but every once in a while I have to step inside one… and I look around and wonder how many kids are in there just like me… staring at the clock and counting down the minutes until they are free.

I would imagine a lot of former prisoners do the same thing when they step back inside a prison.

How did you count down the minutes when you were stuck in that place?

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: in this house we believe...

IN THIS HOUSE WE BELIEVE:

BLACK LIVES MATTER
LOVE IS LOVE
WOMEN'S RIGHTS ARE HUMAN RIGHTS
SCIENCE IS REAL
NO HUMAN IS ILLEGAL
KINDNESS IS EVERYTHING

You've seen it before, or some variation of it. Whether it's slapped onto a lawn sign or an online meme... you've felt your eyes roll to the back of your head when you read the words "kindness is everything" next to "no human is illegal".

What is it about this that makes it lib-coded? Why are you and I filled with second-hand embarrassment and frustration when we read it? What's going on here?

Love is love is gay marriage. Science is real is climate policy. No human is illegal is immigration. Women's rights are human rights is abortion. Black Lives Matter is policing. Kindness is everything is the welfare state.

They are laundering their politics under the banner of reality and decency itself.

This is how our friends, the libs, operate. They don't have politics. They have reality. You have politics. Know what I mean?

Nobody has ever read that sign and changed their mind. It was never meant to do that.

It's a loyalty test.

And if your eyes roll when you read it... you failed.

subject: i picked these two words on purpose

html:
When I first started writing to you, I decided I needed to have a consistent sign-off. Something you would remember me by... something that binds all of the emails together. Makes it feel like we're engaged in a kind of ritual here... because we are. That's what I want these emails to feel like.

There are 10,000 of you who read this, but I don't write to 10,000 people. I write to one. You.

Stay close.

I could have signed off with "Best regards" or "sincerely" or something to that effect, but that's just a pleasantry.

Stay close asks something of you. It tells you there's another one coming. That I consider your attention something of value, something that I want to keep close.

And now, when readers write to me, they often sign off with "I'm staying close".

I made these two words up as a device. But now, it's become part of our connection. It's something you look for, and something I feel is missing until I include it.

And so, I've decided. I want a shirt. Just a black shirt on quality cotton that says "stay close" on the front.

subject: phew
preview: nothing in the grass. probably.
html:
Have you ever watched a lion stalk its prey? It doesn't look like a lion. It looks like grass. That's why the prey usually doesn't figure it out until it's too late. They hear a rustle… they look over… "phew" it's just the wind. They continue doing whatever it was they were doing…

Now another one looks up. It notices the eyes in the grass. It can see the tail on the prowl…

The lion knows it's been noticed. So, what does it do? It doesn't run away. It doesn't say "oh darn, you got me… now I'll leave". No.

The lion decides… "game on".

People hunt this way too... not in the grass, but in language. They use words to cover up the hunt. To make it seem like they're not a threat.

What does that look like?

"We just want everyone to have health care."

"We just want a living wage."

"We just want trans people treated with dignity."

Sound familiar? That's not the wind. That's a predator in the grass getting a read on your herd.

Now, listen to how those same people describe you. There's no benefit of the doubt. You are a racist. A bigot. A fascist. You hate trans people, gays, blacks, immigrants and whatever other 'protected' group they can fire off the top of their head.

It is treated as a given that you always want the worst things and you are always motivated by sinister intentions.

Their gentleness isn't a personality trait. It's a tactic. They are hiding in the grass of soft language.

It was never for you, the Trump supporter. The conservative. You are irredeemable. You are to be hunted, like Charlie.

The soft language is for the rest of the herd… your friends, your neighbors, and anyone else who hasn't looked up yet. The ones who still think "we just want you to have health care" is the wind whistling. Not a lurking predator preparing to devour them.

The people who hated Charlie Kirk told him they just wanted people to have health care.

The problem is, Charlie didn't hear the wind… he saw the predator in the grass. Then he pointed at it so the rest of us could see it. Then it pounced and sunk its teeth into his neck.

But now you see it clearly, right?

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: he turned down $360,000
preview: and he was dead broke at the time
html:
You may have noticed I didn't send you an email yesterday.

That's not because I didn't want to. I sat at my screen for three hours trying to come up with something.

Nothing was coming to me. Everything I wrote felt forced. I couldn't send it to you… it was slop. Writing for the sake of writing. I had nothing to say.

Then, I started browsing YouTube in my frustration… to look for inspiration, but really just feeding my procrastination. Then I stumbled upon a movie trailer for “I Play Rocky”. Have you seen it?

It follows a young Sylvester Stallone trying to get the original Rocky movie made. He was nobody. He couldn't get cast in anything. And a friend told him… "write your own movie and put yourself in it."

So he did. He banged out the first draft in three days, because he wasn't trying to write a screenplay. He was trying to get himself in a movie.

He was offered $360,000 for the script on the condition that a real actor would play Rocky. He said no.

He was broke! And those are 1975 dollars. Everyone thought he was nuts.

In his own words

"If I sold the script and it did well, and I wasn't in it, I would have jumped off a building."

He wasn’t joking. He refused to sell it to them, unless they put him in it. There was no price he would accept. And so they had no choice, but to cast him.

When I read that quote, I realized something.

Rocky wasn’t a character. Rocky was him. Stallone. A nobody that nobody would bet on. Who just wants to be still standing in the end. That’s the spirit of the movie. That also happened to be his life.

He put himself on the page. The writing was straight from his heart. From the pit of his soul.

Meanwhile, I’ve been trying to write an email.

I’ve been trying to find something to tell you about, or come up with some profound point to make…

I was putting pressure on myself... "I have to say something meaningful." "I have to give my readers value." I wasn't writing from the heart and just letting it pour out. That’s where the good stuff lives.

Stallone didn't sit down to write something good. He put himself on the page, and it turned into one of the greatest movies ever made.

I’m not sure this is the greatest email I’ve ever written… actually, I’m sure it’s not. But it’s a window into my process. I am writing myself out of a rut…

I think it worked…

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: should I move on from charlie?

html:
Yesterday I posted about Charlie again on my Sowell page, bringing some more attention to my piece "The Desecration of Charlie Kirk".

As usual, the comments were a mixed bag of supporters praising Charlie, haters spitting on his grave, and conspiracy theorists coming in to tell us what "really happened".

For him, the whole Charlie thing is getting tired. This is what he had to say:

How much longer are you gonna write about Charlie Kirk. We get it, he became a new age martir. But this page writes about it every day. It happened quite a long time ago. Time to move on to more relevant topics of now

This is what I said to him

It hasn't even been a year yet, Matic.

Charlie is the example we learn from.

Your request to stop talking about him and move on has been firmly denied, with all due respect.

~ Clay

We haven't even seen the man accused of killing him go to trial yet. In fact, just today, Judge Graf ruled that the prosecution has enough evidence for the case to finally move forward.

And even once Tyler is found guilty and sentenced, we have to ask... is that justice? What about the flock that's out there picking its next targets as we speak? What about the relentless attacks on his institution, his family, and anyone who says a kind word about him in public?

Should I just move on?

subject: the worst thing you can do in a cave
preview: ... you do it at dinner too
html:
I've been watching claustrophobic cave diving videos on youtube this week. Have you seen those? Somehow I got caught in that algorithm.

I could never do it myself. I'm not even sure why I like the videos. They are genuinely terrifying. My heart rate goes up while I'm watching a man get stuck in a hole he can barely fit through, desperately trying to get through to the other side so he doesn't just die right there. And on the other side, by the way, there is another hellish obstacle to overcome.

It's a thrill just to watch it. Better than any horror movie. And much like a horror movie, it's a scenario I never want to find myself in. If I were to live a billion years, I would go caving 0 times. No thank you.

That feeling I get watching these videos isn't foreign to me. It's familiar. It's a genuine fear response.

It's the same feeling I often get when I find myself in a hostile political argument, particularly if it's with someone I care about, or in front of an audience.

Heart rate rises… can't think so clearly anymore. Panic sets in. I have to do something to get out of this! You know exactly what I'm talking about, right? You've felt it too.

My brain is processing this moment as danger. As if I were stuck in a cave. Why?

Because it is dangerous… just not in the same way the cave is. Do you have anyone in your life that you stopped saying certain things around? If you do, then you know what I mean.

The relationship is still there, it's just smaller than what it was before. It becomes harder, maybe even impossible to let this person see your true self without sabotaging the whole thing.

It feels like a looming threat, because it is one. Your body notices this, even if you don't.

It doesn't want to be ostracized from the community… historically that was a literal death sentence. So your body processes a serious political disagreement with another member of the tribe as a life-threatening situation. That's why you panic.

Do you know what the professional cave divers say is the worst thing you can do when you're stuck in a cave? Panic. That's the thing that'll get you killed for sure. They all say it.

Panic in a cave is obvious. You thrash about, burn through your air, have a heart attack… and die.

The ones who make it out don't say they chose to thrash. They admit they panicked, they got scared, and they thought they were going to die.

Panic in a political argument doesn't look like thrashing. It looks like whatever gets you out of the situation the fastest. Get nasty, passive aggressive, call them a moron… be generally unpleasant. Stay quiet, and let it die. Tell them you "agree to disagree" and move on. Make a joke.

And afterward, we aren't so honest about it. We come up with all kinds of excuses. We try to tell a story that doesn't make us feel embarrassed. That doesn't make us admit we were scared. Panicking.

I see it all the time. I've seen it myself. I still do.

But I'm aware of it now. And just like those cave divers on YouTube, I know what's happening, while it's happening. That takes about half of the stress away. Not all of it, but enough to think.

When you panic in political conversations, you are killing your reputation. People can smell it on you. You can smell it on others. It doesn't matter how right you are, it matters how you behave.

This is how Trump has won almost every political debate he's ever been in, even when he's completely wrong. He knows the game. He doesn't panic. He sets the stage, and makes them panic instead.

Charlie was good at this too. He sat in front of hostile crowds for years and never once looked like he wanted out of the room.

Look for the people who can do this. Follow their example.

Don't be a panican.

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: i hadn't swung a golf club in over a decade
preview: yesterday that changed
html:
Last night I hung out with the boys. Some of the guys I grew up with as a kid. Old friends I almost never see anymore, but still think of as brothers.

It was a legendary night. We had some of the biggest laughs I’ve had in years… it was just one of those really great moments in time that is good for your soul, you know what I mean?

3 of the 4 of us had just played a golf tournament that day. My Uncles annual tournament that he puts on for fun. This was the 48th year. Isn’t that something?

Until yesterday, I hadn’t played golf in over a decade. I regret missing all of those years now. I had such a great time.

One of the most fascinating things to me was the nature of the political conversation that took place. For context, this is in Ontario, Canada, the heart of the great Lake America troll operation currently being executed by everybody’s favorite President.

You would think that I’d hear some complaints. Some of the typical Trump Derangement stuff, you know? There was something like 50 people at this tournament, and a lot of wealthy boomers. I know the libs were among us… but they didn’t make a peep.

Then there was Max, my cousins lifelong best friend. His bro, so to speak. At one point, at the afterparty he just went on a whole drunken comedy routine about the Lake America thing and everybody around was laughing. Nobody cared about it at all, other than the fact that it was funny.

If someone cared, they didn’t dare to make it known, for they would risk becoming part of the punchline.

This is not what I expected going into this thing. I expected to have to watch what I say around certain people, I don’t want to create a problem at a fun family gathering, you know? But nope.

Something is changing. Or maybe this is just a tiny meaningless anecdote. Because when I look at the media, or the polls telling me what my countrymen supposedly care about… I don't recognize the people I was standing with on Saturday.

Look at poor Doug Ford. Brother of the late, legendary Rob Ford, Mayor of Toronto. Current Premier of Ontario. (that’s kind of like a Governor)

It’s a pitiful sight really... I almost feel bad having to tell you about this.

He put up a sign. Custom-made. Twenty-four feet wide, standing on six foot legs…

It reads “Lake Ontario. Now and Always.”

He stood in front of it, and declared

“We'll never, ever back down from a bully.”

“Everything's on the table right now, absolutely everything. We need to get a deal, a fair deal.”

Does any of this read as strength to you? Notice who's leading the conversation here, and who's perpetually in a defensive posture.

Do you think Doug ever considered that this is exactly the reaction Trump wanted?

Does the fish think before it bites the worm?

He did all of this on Saturday. While I was out laughing at Max’s drunken Lake America routine, Doug Ford was putting on his super serious face, trying to tell us how not funny it is.

Sorry Doug. We were all laughing.

stay close,

~ Clay

subject: my dad the mechanic
preview: and the one receipt i've never been able to check
html:
I'm not a mechanic. My dad is, and he's the guy I run to whenever my car starts making a funny noise or needs some kind of diagnostic. He’s saved me countless thousands of dollars over the years.

I come to my dad because he has very specific knowledge and experience in this field. He’s a professional... people paid him for it.

Do you know who I don’t run to for answers? People who aren’t mechanics. People who have no knowledge and experience in this field.

Seems obvious, right?

When I need an oil change, I don’t run to the hospital to find a nurse. I don’t ask the guy in the McDonald's drive-through window where the oil filter is in a 2013 Yaris.

I go straight to the people who have the demonstrated knowledge and experience in this field. Then, I pay them, and give them skin in the game. They are now invested in the outcome of my car through a contract.

This is how the market works. It’s not just mechanics... pick whatever specialized trade you want… surgeons, pilots, plumbers… these are people who took the time to acquire specialized knowledge and experience, and then by taking on work they have real skin in the game. Real responsibility.

Nobody thinks this is controversial. In fact, you might be wondering what point I’m even getting at. I’m just saying plainly obvious things, right?

Nobody calls you an elitist for wanting a licensed pilot, and nobody calls you cruel for asking where the surgeon was trained.

We do this everywhere, every day. Even when we’re making decisions as mundane as buying a new TV. We look at reviews from people who bought the same one, we read an article by a professional tech writer, and take whatever measures we need to make us feel comfortable handing over our money. The thing we work so hard for.

All this for a TV.

But when it comes to selecting the rulers of our country? The people who make the rules we all live by, and get to decide how all of our taxes get spent?… Well, for these most important decisions we have something called Universal Suffrage.

You don’t have to have any experience, no demonstrated knowledge, no real skin in the game… and if you choose badly? Nothing really happens to you. You get no feedback that you did something wrong, in fact, the opposite. You can find countless people telling you that you did it right and it’s “those other guys” who voted the other way who did something wrong.

A mechanic who wrecks your engine hears about it. The surgeon who takes out your kidney when they were supposed to be operating on your heart gets a lawsuit. That's how they got good in the first place.

The voter never finds out.

You’ll spend an entire evening, maybe more, on the television. Reviews, a professional write-up, maybe a few youtube videos, and a trip to the store to compare them with your own eyes.

You’re spending real money that you worked hard for, you don’t want to throw it away on junk. There’s a cost. You have to live with that junk.

The government doesn’t work like this.

If you're a working class taxpayer, the government will take more from you this year than you spent on that television, and you'll never see a line item for a penny of it.

You don't bother checking if you're getting a good return on that money. When you buy the TV you get a receipt down the exact penny of exactly what it cost you, and what you got in return. $728 for the TV. $22.35 for HDMI cables, $125 for insurance… whatever you chose.

This is a contract. If the supplier fails to make good on any of those items you have a legal claim against them. They owe you.

None of this depended on you doing your homework. The man who walks in and buys the first one he sees without thinking or doing any research gets the same receipt, the same warranty, the same fourteen days to bring it back, and the same court if it burns his house down.

He didn’t earn any of it... it’s just part of the deal.

Now think about the other one. Your relationship as a taxpayer to the government.

No receipt, no itemized list showing precisely where your money went. No contract with clear terms where you can seek resolution in a court if you don’t believe the government is living up to its end of the contract.

There’s no contract. You pay what they say you owe, or you go to jail.

And so, you pay. Because you’re not self-destructive and you want to go on with your life. You never find out if any of it was worth it. You don’t bother looking for the receipt and checking to see if you got a good deal, because you know that’s not really how this works.

So what’s my point?

I want you to understand the type of game you’re playing when you enter the political arena. There’s no reason and there’s no accountability to the truth.

It’s the only transaction in your life where you hand over the money first, get no accounting of where it went, and have no way to complain if the answer turns out to be nowhere. And you can’t walk away from it.

You don’t have to buy the new television. You have to pay your taxes… or else.

And so, understand this. Politics is not a marketplace of ideas. It is war.
